strengths: Well-motivated practical problem addressing the challenge of monitoring deployed models with limited labeled data
Rigorous theoretical contributions including assumption-free false alarm guarantees (Theorem 3.2) and proven unbiasedness of PPRM estimates (Lemma 3.1)
Clever adaptive hyperparameter selection mechanism (Lemma 3.3) with practical sliding-window implementation that shows empirical benefits
Comprehensive experimental validation across three diverse domains (image classification, LLM monitoring, telecommunications) with multiple baselines
Demonstrated robustness across varying predictor quality (Figure 4) and both external and self-synthetic labeling strategies
Clear bridge between fully supervised (SRM) and purely unsupervised (URM) approaches, addressing limitations of both
Sound technical execution with proper probability union bounds and confidence sequence construction
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing PPI and SRM techniques with straightforward theoretical proofs that follow directly from Lemma 2.2
Insufficient guidance on critical hyperparameter selection: window length L, η_max, and δ allocation lack principled justification or sensitivity analysis
Unrealistic experimental distribution shifts: gradually increasing Gaussian noise and prompt complexity do not reflect real-world shift patterns; missing established benchmarks like PACS or VLCS
Modest empirical improvements: time-to-alarm gains of 30-50 steps over SRM are relatively small; missing statistical significance testing and confidence intervals

Incomplete analysis of predictor quality requirements: no characterization of how degraded a predictor can be before method fails; self-synthetic strategy vulnerable when deployed model is severely degraded
Normalization scheme (Eq. 22) lacks theoretical justification: affine transformation g_a(·) could introduce bias or affect bound tightness, not analyzed
Running average risk definition (R̄_t) dilutes early performance degradation; no discussion of alternatives or sensitivity to this design choice
Missing reproducibility details: number of runs, random seed selection, precise error bar computation (full range is ambiguous) not specified
Covariance dependence in optimal η*_t: limited insight into when Cov(u_t, ũ_t) is high/low; no diagnostic tools provided
Incomplete practical guidance: methods for choosing ε_tol and δ allocation not provided; computational cost and scalability analysis absent
Limited comparison scope: missing engagement with drift detection literature (DDM, ADWIN) and broader domain adaptation/concept drift methods
No failure analysis: conditions under which PPRM performs poorly or fails not discussed; robustness to concept drift in predictor not addressed

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated practical problem of monitoring deployed models with limited labeled data
Provides rigorous assumption-free false-alarm guarantees through Theorem 3.2
Elegant theoretical result (Lemma 3.1) establishing unbiasedness of PPI estimates independent of hyperparameter choice
Principled approach to adaptive hyperparameter selection via variance minimization (Lemma 3.3)
Diverse experimental evaluation across three domains (vision, LLM, telecommunications)
Clear connection to existing frameworks (SRM and PPI) with solid mathematical foundation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is mechanical application of existing PPI techniques to SRM framework; Theorem 3.2 proof is trivial (literally 'follows from Lemma 2.2')
Modest empirical improvements barely exceeding experimental noise: ~5-10% faster alarm detection with substantial error bar overlap; no statistical significance testing provided
Unrealistic assumption of guaranteed labeled data availability at every time step (n_t≥1); this is stronger than 'limited labeled data' and poorly justified versus purely unsupervised approaches
Incomplete baseline comparisons: URM missing from most experiments without explanation; no fair cost-benefit analysis since PPRM gets both labeled and unlabeled data while SRM gets only labeled
Critical underdeveloped insight from Figure 4: PPRM only helps for medium-quality predictors; when f_p is strong (GPT-4.1), improvements vanish; practitioners lack guidance on when to use PPRM
Artificial experimental setups with no naturally occurring shifts; only Gaussian noise, prompt complexity changes tested; generalization to label shift, concept drift unclear
Self-synthetic variant (Figure 2b) most practical but severely underdeveloped with only one experiment
No ablation studies on key hyperparameters: window length L chosen arbitrarily (L=60) without sensitivity analysis; missing ablations on L, η_0, δ allocation
Theorem 3.2 provides no characterization of when PPRM beats SRM or variance reduction bounds; theoretical contribution is shallow despite mathematical rigor
Computational overhead not discussed: PPRM requires predictions on all unlabeled samples; runtime comparison with SRM absent
Plug-in estimator for η_t (Eq. 27) could be significantly biased during non-stationary periods or with limited historical data; no finite-sample bias analysis provided
Statistical rigor concerns: error bars show full range not standard error; no significance testing; experimental details sparse (random seeds, number of runs)
LLM experiments problematic: risk threshold artificially low (0.35 out of 0.30-0.55 range); only one deployed model tested (Qwen2-VL-2B); reliability of LLM-as-judge not discussed
Paper structure priorities misplaced: telecommunications example with promising self-synthetic results relegated to appendix

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: Addresses the important gap between fully supervised monitoring (SRM) with scarce labels and purely unsupervised approaches that require strong assumptions.

Sound theoretical framework: Lemma 3.1 establishes unbiasedness of PPI-based estimates; Theorem 3.2 provides rigorous assumption-free false-alarm guarantees without requiring auxiliary model error rate assumptions (unlike prior work).
Principled adaptive hyperparameter selection: Lemma 3.3 derives optimal variance-minimizing η values, with empirical validation showing 3-5% improvement in detection time (Table 1).
Comprehensive multi-domain experiments: Validation spans vision (CIFAR10-C), NLP (LLM QA on MMLU/CMExam), and telecommunications with both external predictors and self-synthetic strategies.
Practical flexibility: Framework accommodates various predictor types (deployed model, LLM-as-judge, external models) without assumptions on their accuracy.
Clear presentation: Well-organized paper with intuitive figures, clear problem formulation, and logical flow from motivation to theory to experiments.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contribution combines existing PPI and SRM frameworks; optimal ηt selection directly follows from PPI++ (Angelopoulos et al., 2023b). While useful, incremental technical contribution limits impact.

Predominantly synthetic distribution shifts: CIFAR10-C uses programmatic Gaussian noise; LLM experiments create shifts by selecting harder prompts from another model. Real-world distribution shifts may exhibit different characteristics; robustness unclear.

Practical constraint on labeled data: Requires ≥1 labeled sample per timestep (nt > 0), which somewhat contradicts the 'scarce labeled data' motivation. Behavior with sporadic or batched labeling is unexplored.

Underspecified hyperparameter selection: Window length L=60 lacks sensitivity analysis; ηmax for affine normalization not clearly specified; limited guidance for practitioners on setting these values.

Theory-practice gap on detection time: Lemma 3.3 optimizes one-step variance, but detection time depends on cumulative behavior. No sample complexity bounds or formal characterization of detection delay provided.
Insufficient failure analysis: When does PPRM underperform SRM? How does performance vary with different shift types (covariate, label shift)? Long-term drift behavior unexplored.
Limited baseline comparisons: Only compares to SRM and URM; missing comparisons with other recent distribution shift detection methods or semi-supervised monitoring approaches.

Reproducibility concerns: Code availability not mentioned; some experimental details underspecified (exact prompt modifications, precise shift magnitudes); betting algorithm implementation details missing.
Fixed small-scale regime: Uses 1 labeled + 15 unlabeled per timestep; robustness to different data ratios or realistic labeling patterns not explored.
Missing practical guidance on predictor quality: Figure 4 shows empirical relationship between predictor accuracy and detection time, but no formal characterization or worst-case analysis.

strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem—monitoring deployed models with limited labeled data—that is highly relevant to practitioners
Provides rigorous assumption-free type-I error guarantees (Theorem 3.2) while extending supervised risk monitoring to the semi-supervised setting
Develops a principled adaptive mechanism to optimize reliance on unlabeled data (Lemma 3.3, Eq. 27) with clear empirical benefits (Table 1)
Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse domains (vision, LLMs, telecommunications) with proper false-alarm rate validation (Figure 5) and extensive ablations
Technically sound proofs and correct application of prediction-powered inference framework to sequential monitoring
Flexibility to use deployed model itself for synthetic labels, enabling practical deployment without auxiliary models
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—the core contribution is a straightforward application of existing PPI framework to SRM; Theorem 3.2 follows directly from combining Lemma 3.1 with SRM's existing theory, and Lemma 3.1 is standard PPI unbiasedness

Inadequate treatment of synthetic label quality: Figure 12 shows PPRM underperforms SRM with poor predictors, contradicting 'no assumptions' claims; lacks finite-sample bounds relating predictor accuracy to detection performance
All experiments assume labeled data availability at every time step (n_t ≥ 1); never tests the critical scenario when labels become scarce/unavailable, weakening the 'semi-supervised' claim

Empirical improvements are often modest (e.g., ~40 timesteps faster than SRM in Figure 3 out of 500+ total, with wide confidence intervals), and no systematic analysis of sample complexity or minimum labeled data requirements

Theoretical detection delay analysis (Proposition A.1) is highly restrictive, covering only binary Bernoulli risks in stationary regime; does not address realistic continuous, non-stationary settings or provide lower bounds
Adaptive hyperparameter selection (L=60) appears ad-hoc; Figure 10 shows substantial sensitivity to window length L with no principled guidance provided for practitioners

Incomplete comparison with related work: prediction-powered e-values (Csillag et al., 2025) mentioned but not experimentally compared; unclear guidance on when to use PPRM vs. URM across different scenarios

Missing critical ablations: no analysis of label noise robustness, handling of correlated predictor/model failures, or behavior under rapid distribution shifts; cost-benefit analysis versus collecting more labels not provided
